On this page

The Function Context ​

A server function reaches the platform through ctx: databases, prompts, secrets and config vars, live sends and channels, invitations, email, analytics and outside services. This page covers each of those calls and the few capabilities a function declares for them.

Calling the platform from a function ​

ctx gives a function access to app data and services. Function code runs with the app’s authority, regardless of the caller’s permissions. ctx.user identifies the caller for attribution; it is null when a trigger starts the function. Use the function’s authorize method to control who may call it.

ts
import { defineFunction, requireSignedIn } from "primitive-functions";

export default defineFunction({
  input: ["db3Id", "taskId"],
  authorize: requireSignedIn(),
  handler: async (input: { db3Id: string; taskId: string }, ctx) => {
    // Reads the database whoever holds it; the caller's own access does not enter.
    const task = await ctx.db3(input.db3Id, "workspace").model("tasks").get(input.taskId);
    return { title: task?.title ?? null, askedBy: ctx.user?.userId ?? null };
  },
});

When the function accepts a resource ID from a caller, check whether that caller is allowed to use the resource before acting on it.

Checking a user's access ​

A function can read and write every database in its app, so a database id that arrives in the input is a claim, not a permission. Check the caller's access in authorize before the handler runs. auth.db3(id, type).permissions() answers the caller's level on a database — reader, read-write or owner — or null when they have none:

ts
import { allow, defineFunction, deny } from "primitive-functions";

export default defineFunction("rename-project", {
  input: ["db3Id", "name"],
  authorize: async (input: { db3Id: string; name: string }, auth) => {
    if (!auth.user) return deny("FORBIDDEN");
    const level = await auth.db3(input.db3Id, "project").permissions();
    // A content write needs a real grant; an app role is not one.
    return level === "read-write" || level === "owner" ? allow() : deny("FORBIDDEN");
  },
  handler: async (input, ctx) => {
    await ctx.db3(input.db3Id, "project").model("settings").patch("main", { data: { name: input.name } });
    return { renamed: true };
  },
});

auth.db3(id, type).publicAccess() answers "reader" while the database is public and the app's signedOutAccess is on, and null otherwise; it answers the same for every caller, signed out included. requireDb3Level and requirePublicDb3 build both checks into one line — see Serving a database named by the caller.

To check another user — or the caller from inside the handler — call ctx.api.db3.validateAccess:

ts
const access = await ctx.api.db3.validateAccess({ db3Id: input.db3Id, body: { userId: input.memberId } });
// { hasAccess: true, permission: "read-write", accessSource: "group" }

Both resolve the user's effective access the way the database enforces it: direct grants, groups, collections, link access and app access. A database with sync off grants no member access, so both answer none for it — a sync-off database is reached only through your functions, which decide access from what your app records (see Serving a sync-off database through functions).

Which user a call is about ​

Some calls are about one user: a member's collections, their agent sessions. Each takes userId. Omitted, it means the caller; a userId that is empty, null or not a user id throws SUBJECT_USER_INVALID, so leave it out rather than passing "" for "me". A function that cron, a webhook or --as system started has no caller, so it names the member — leaving userId out there throws FUNCTION_SUBJECT_REQUIRED rather than answering for nobody:

ts
import { allowCallers, defineFunction, requireSignedIn } from "primitive-functions";

export default defineFunction({
  input: ["userId"],
  authorize: allowCallers({ webhook: true, cron: true, manual: true, users: requireSignedIn() }),
  handler: async (input: { userId: string }, ctx) => {
    const collections = await ctx.api.collections.list({ userId: input.userId });
    return { collections: collections.items.length };
  },
});

The same rule covers collections.list, ctx.agents, and db3.aliases.set, resolve and delete, where userId is optional (set takes it in its body). The reads that name a member in their path require it: collections.listForUser, groups.listUserMemberships, and db3.listHeldByUser and db3.listSharedWithUser, which list the databases a member holds and those shared with them. The two database listings take tag and type to keep only matching databases; a filtered page can come back short or empty with hasMore: true, so follow nextCursor until hasMore is false. App-wide reads such as users.list take no user.

Who may name a user other than the caller depends on how the function was started, and the role is read at each call:

RunuserId omittedAnother member
No caller (cron, webhook, --as system)FUNCTION_SUBJECT_REQUIREDAllowed
Invoked by an app owner or adminThe callerAllowed
Invoked by any other memberThe callerSUBJECT_USER_FORBIDDEN
Invoked by any other member, from a function declaring users:readAny or users:actAsAnyThe callerAllowed for the calls its grant covers
An agent's tool, context or history function, and anything it startsThe turn's initiatorSUBJECT_USER_FORBIDDEN

A function whose own code chooses the member — a teacher's remove-member reading a student's memberships to see whether they are enrolled in another class — declares that in its TOML, as described in Naming other members. Without that declaration, a user id that arrives in a request body, a prompt or a model's tool arguments can never reach another member's data through these calls. On the calls where userId is optional, a named user who is not a member of the app throws SUBJECT_USER_NOT_FOUND, and so does ctx.usage.forUser. Of the other reads that require a userId, groups.listUserMemberships answers an empty list and the rest a plain 404 with no code.

ctx.api.collections.listForUser({ userId }) pages through the collections a member belongs to, each with their permission; loop on hasMore, not on the number of items, since a page can be short or empty while hasMore is true. A function with no caller, or one an app owner or admin invoked, may list any member's collections, so keep such a function behind an admin-only authorize or a trigger.

ctx.api.users.setProfile sets a member's display name and avatar. Pass the fields to change in body; avatarUrl is an http: or https: URL, and null clears the avatar. It answers { userId, email, name, avatarUrl }:

ts
await ctx.api.users.setProfile({
  userId: input.userId,
  body: { name: input.name, avatarUrl: input.avatarUrl },
});

Gotchas

  • Calls that hand something to a user — users.setProfile and ctx.channels.authorize — are outside this rule and accept any member. A tool that passes a model-supplied user id to users.setProfile changes that user's profile, so check the id first.
  • ctx.channels.authorize with no caller and no userId keeps its own code, FUNCTION_CHANNEL_GRANTEE_REQUIRED.

Use ctx.prompts.run for prompts and ctx.integrations.call for external services. Direct internet requests are not allowed.

Reading and writing user properties ​

ctx.users.get(userId) reads a member with their declared properties, defaults applied; null for a user who is not a member of this app:

ts
const member = await ctx.users.get(input.userId);
return { plan: member?.properties.plan ?? null };

ctx.users.getBy(name, value) finds the member who holds a unique property's value, or a named [[unique_constraints]] entry's values (an array in declared order, or an object by field name); null when nobody holds it.

ctx.users.setProperties(userId, patch, options?) is a merge-patch — each named field is set, null clears it back to its default — and addToSet/removeFromSet add or remove one or more members of a stringset field. Pass condition to write only when the user, as stored, matches a filter over properties.* and the base fields userId/email/name/avatarUrl (not role or status — re-read the membership instead):

ts
await ctx.users.setProperties(
  input.userId,
  { plan: "pro" },
  { condition: { "properties.plan": "free" } }
);

A failed write throws a PrimitivePlatformError whose errorCode is USER_PROPERTY_UNKNOWN (undeclared name), USER_PROPERTY_INVALID (wrong type or over a cap), USER_PROPERTY_UNIQUE_CONFLICT (another user holds the value), USER_PROPERTY_CONDITION_FAILED (the condition didn't hold), or USER_PROPERTY_NOT_CLIENT_WRITABLE (a client session named a field it may not write — functions always may). Two calls patching different fields of the same user both land, even run at the same time.

ctx.users.list(options?) and iterate(options?) page the app's roster directly — limit, capped at 100, and a cursor; iterate repeats list as an AsyncIterable, for a request function or a single-slice loop only (a durable loop still takes its own pages inside step.do, with an explicit cursor, since a memoized step does not advance an iterator on resume). Both keep working and take no filter, but are soft-deprecated: prefer ctx.users.query to filter, sort or page up to 1,000 at once, and ctx.users.forEachBatch to run a function over every match instead of paging by hand.

ctx.users.query, count and aggregate filter, sort and aggregate over the app's users from a separate index that trails a write by seconds, rather than reading the live record — see Querying users, below, and The Consistency Contract for which calls read which side.

ctx.invitations.getBy(name, value) finds a pending invitation by a unique value its initialProperties will give the invitee at signup — see Invitations.

Querying users ​

ctx.users.query, count and aggregate accept the same filter grammar as a records query, over the base fields (userId, email, name, avatarUrl, role, status, addedAt, testUser) and properties.<name>, and page up to 1,000 at a time:

ts
const page = await ctx.users.query({
  filter: { role: "member", "properties.plan": "pro" },
  sort: { addedAt: -1 },
  limit: 50,
});
const { count } = await ctx.users.count({ filter: { "properties.plan": "pro" } });
const { result } = await ctx.users.aggregate({
  operations: [{ type: "count" }],
  groupBy: ["properties.plan"],
});

include is refused: a search answer carries only the base fields and declared properties. Each answer's meta.scans names a filter or sort field the index could not serve from an index — an undeclared property, or one not declared indexed — so you can see when a query is doing a full scan.

Reading and writing databases ​

ctx.db3(db3Id, "<type>").model("<model>") reads and writes one model of one database:

ts
import { defineFunction, requireSignedIn } from "primitive-functions";

export default defineFunction({
  input: ["db3Id"],
  authorize: requireSignedIn(),
  handler: async (input: { db3Id: string }, ctx) => {
    const orders = ctx.db3(input.db3Id, "orders").model("orders");
    const open = await orders.query({ filter: { status: "open" }, sort: { createdAt: -1 } });

    // Every record a read hands back carries its id.
    await orders.patch(open.items[0].id, { data: { status: "picked" } });
    return { open: open.items.length };
  },
});

What the handle promises:

  • The app's authority. Every call acts as the app, on any database in it — synced or not, whoever holds it. The caller needs no grant and the function declares nothing; check the caller in authorize when they chose the database (above).
  • Typed from your types. primitive config push (or primitive functions codegen) types the Db3 namespace of functions/primitive.d.ts from db3-types/, so the second argument accepts only a type you declared, .model() only a model that type declares, and rows come back typed — a type's timestamps as required numbers on the models it stamps, which writes leave out. A write takes null on any field the model leaves optional, with no cast: patch(id, { data: { note: null } }) stores null in place of the value and doesn't remove the field (see Null and unset fields). A required field refuses null. Each model also gets a filter and a sort type (below). The type argument is checked at compile time only; the server enforces the database's actual type. See Generating code.
  • Untyped databases. Omit the type for a database created without one: ctx.db3(id).model("notes") gives the same handle over untyped rows.
  • As a member. Pass { asUser: userId } as the third argument to judge every call by that member's grant instead of the app's authority — a database with sync off then refuses them. Naming anyone but the caller needs the users:actAsAny capability.
  • Refusals reject. A database that doesn't exist in the app — never created, or deleted — rejects every call with DB3_NOT_FOUND (404); get on a missing record answers null instead. A failed condition rejects with DB3_CONDITION_NOT_MET (409). The condition is checked first, so a patch or delete with a condition on a missing record is that 409, with details.current.row null. Without a condition, a patch on a missing record rejects with DB3_RECORD_NOT_FOUND (404) and a delete does nothing. An increment on a missing record is always DB3_RECORD_NOT_FOUND (404), condition or not. A rule in the type that refuses the write rejects with DB3_TRIGGER_REFUSED (409), its code in details.reason, and a model the type doesn't declare with DB3_MODEL_NOT_DECLARED (400). Two of these are 409s, so branch on code, not status.
  • Retries apply once. A write that timed out may have applied; resend it with the same requestId and it applies once.

The handle offers get, query, count, aggregate, save, patch, delete, increment, batch, batchRead, deleteWhere and patchWhere; ctx.db3(db3Id, type).batch([...]) spans several models in one transaction, and batchRead([...]) answers several reads from one state of the database, each result typed by the read at its position (a query read's rows are that model's). deleteWhere({ filter }) and patchWhere({ filter, data }) change up to 1,000 records matching a filter in one call; loop on nextCursor until hasMore is false (Changing every record that matches a filter). Each operation, with its server function example, is on Reading and Writing Records. query answers 100 records when limit is omitted and takes a limit up to 10,000; a page also stops before 8 MiB of records, so loop on hasMore. An include can nest up to 3 levels, and a hasMany include reads at most 1,000 related records per request; past either budget the read is refused with DB3_PAGE_TOO_LARGE. The rest of the bounds are under Limits.

To create a database, or to change who holds it, its sync or its app access, a function uses ctx.api.db3 with the matching capability — see Sharing and Access. To run a function whenever a database of a type changes, declare a database change trigger.

Loading many records at once ​

To write thousands of records in one call — a first sync from an outside service, a page of a ledger — use load on the database handle. It sends the rows as one bulk load and waits for the database to apply them:

ts
import { defineFunction, requireSignedIn } from "primitive-functions";

export default defineFunction({
  input: ["db3Id", "transactions"],
  authorize: requireSignedIn(),
  handler: async (input: { db3Id: string; transactions: Array<{ id: string; amount: number }> }, ctx) => {
    const ledger = ctx.db3(input.db3Id, "ledger");
    const result = await ledger.load(
      input.transactions.map((t) => ({ model: "transactions", id: t.id, patch: { amount: t.amount } }))
    );
    // The wait ran out first: the load goes on, and loadStatus reads it later.
    if (!result.done) return { pending: result.sessionId };
    return { applied: result.applied, refused: result.refusedRows };
  },
});
  • Rows. Each row names a model, a record id and a patch of that model's fields; { _deleted: true } on its own deletes the record. Rows may come in any order and span models, naming each record once. On a typed handle a wrong model or field type is a compile error.
  • Options. mode: "refresh" also removes the records of the rows' models (and of any models you list) that no row names. waitMs is how long the call waits after sending the rows: 20,000 ms by default, at most 600,000 ms, 0 to return at once.
  • The result. state ends "complete", "failed" (with failure) or "aborted", and done is then true. applied counts the rows the database took, refusedRows the rows it refused (a type mismatch, a unique-key collision), and refused names the first 20.
  • Later reads. loadStatus(sessionId) answers the same result again, and loadRefused(sessionId, { limit, cursor }) pages every refused row.

Gotchas

  • The wait ends before the invocation does. It stops 1,000 ms before the function's deadline, so a request function on the default 5 s timeout often returns done: false. Return the sessionId and read loadStatus from a later call, or raise timeoutMs; run a load of many thousands of rows as a task.
  • One load at a time. A second load on a database while another is still being sent or applied rejects with DOCUMENT_INGEST_ACTIVE (409). An invocation that times out while it is still sending its rows leaves that load open until it expires, and loads on the database are refused until then.
  • Bad rows reject before anything is sent. A record named twice, an invalid id or model name, a patch that is not an object, or a waitMs out of range rejects with code DB3_LOAD_INVALID, naming the row or option. So does load on a handle opened with asUser: a load runs on the app's own authority.

Helpers that work on any model ​

A helper that pages through any model takes the handle as Db3ModelHandle<T>. T follows the model you pass, so the rows come back typed:

ts
import { defineFunction, requireSignedIn, type Db3ModelHandle } from "primitive-functions";

async function readAllRows<T>(model: Db3ModelHandle<T>, filter: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<T[]> {
  const rows: T[] = [];
  let cursor: string | undefined;
  do {
    const page = await model.query({ filter, cursor, limit: 1000 });
    rows.push(...page.items);
    cursor = page.hasMore ? page.nextCursor : undefined;
  } while (cursor);
  return rows;
}

export default defineFunction({
  input: ["db3Id"],
  authorize: requireSignedIn(),
  handler: async (input: { db3Id: string }, ctx) => {
    const orders = ctx.db3(input.db3Id, "orders").model("orders");
    const unpicked = await readAllRows(orders, { pickedAt: null });
    return { unpicked: unpicked.length };
  },
});

A helper can take the model's name instead, generic over the type's model names. primitive-functions exports the types it is written with, each keyed by the database type: Db3TypeModelName<"orders"> (the model names), Db3TypeRow<"orders", M> (a row), Db3TypeFilter<"orders", M> and Db3TypeSort<"orders", M> (a caller's filter and sort), and Db3TypeBatchOp<"orders", M> (one batch write, any model's when M is left out):

ts
import { type Db3TypeBatchOp, type Db3TypeFilter, type Db3TypeModelName, type Db3TypeRow, type FunctionContext } from "primitive-functions";

async function readAll<M extends Db3TypeModelName<"orders">>(
  ctx: FunctionContext, db3Id: string, model: M, filter: Db3TypeFilter<"orders", M>
): Promise<Array<Db3TypeRow<"orders", M>>> {
  const rows: Array<Db3TypeRow<"orders", M>> = [];
  let cursor: string | undefined;
  do {
    const page = await ctx.db3(db3Id, "orders").model(model).query({ filter, sort: { id: 1 }, cursor, limit: 1000 });
    rows.push(...page.items);
    cursor = page.hasMore ? page.nextCursor : undefined;
  } while (cursor);
  return rows;
}

async function writeInChunks(ctx: FunctionContext, db3Id: string, ops: Array<Db3TypeBatchOp<"orders">>) {
  const db = ctx.db3(db3Id, "orders");
  for (let at = 0; at < ops.length; at += 100) await db.batch(ops.slice(at, at + 100));
}

// At the call site the model is known: the rows are orders, and the filter is checked against them.
const unpicked = await readAll(ctx, db3Id, "orders", { pickedAt: null });

A Db3TypeBatchOp's data is checked against the model its model names.

Gotchas

  • A literal inside the helper must suit every model. A filter or sort written inside a generic helper, such as { status: "open" }, is checked against every model the name may be: it is a mismatch (below) when one of them refuses it, for example when that model gives status another kind. Take the filter as a Db3TypeFilter parameter instead, so each call site is checked against its own model.
  • A literal upsertOn inside the helper is refused. The helper doesn't know which model's unique names apply. Pass the name in as a string.
  • The database handle's batch needs a literal model name.Db3TypeBatchOp<"orders", M> with M a type parameter is refused by ctx.db3(id, "orders").batch(ops). Build the op with a literal model name, take already-built ops as a parameter typed Db3TypeBatchOp<"orders"> (no model parameter), or pass the M-typed ops to the model handle's .model(model).batch(ops) instead.

Typed filters and sorts ​

A ctx.db3(id, "<type>").model("<Model>") handle knows its model's declared fields, so config push checks the filters and sorts you pass to query, count and aggregate: a declared field must get an operator and a value its kind takes.

ts
import { defineFunction, requireSignedIn } from "primitive-functions";

export default defineFunction({
  input: ["db3Id"],
  authorize: requireSignedIn(),
  handler: async (input: { db3Id: string }, ctx) => {
    const orders = ctx.db3(input.db3Id, "orders").model("orders");
    const open = await orders.query({
      filter: { status: "open", total: { $gte: 10 }, tags: { $contains: "rush" } },
      sort: { createdAt: -1 },
    });
    const shipped = await orders.count({ filter: { status: "shipped" } });
    return { open: open.items.length, shipped: shipped.count };
  },
});

In this release a mismatch through the handle, such as $startsWith on a number, is a push warning: config push prints the compiler's diagnostic and the function still ships. A later release refuses it.

The handle checks the name an upsert takes the same way: a save's upsertOn and a batch upsert's constraint must be one of the model's unique fields or named unique constraints. A name held in a string variable is not checked.

For each model, functions/primitive.d.ts also declares Db3.<Model>Filter, Db3.<Model>Sort and Db3.<Model>Unique, the names an upsert takes. A value annotated with them is checked now: config push refuses a mismatch in it.

ts
import type { Db3 } from "./primitive";

const filter: Db3.OrdersFilter = { total: { $gte: 10 } };
const sort: Db3.OrdersSort = { createdAt: -1 };
const key: Db3.OrdersUnique = "orderNumber"; // a field declared unique

To make the handle's mismatches errors now too, add a declaration file under functions/, such as functions/db3-strict.d.ts:

ts
export {};
declare module "primitive-functions" { interface Db3FilterTyping { enforced: true } }

A declared field takes the operators of its kind:

KindOperators
string$eq, $ne, $in, $nin, $exists, $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $startsWith, $endsWith, $containsText, $all, $size
number$eq, $ne, $in, $nin, $exists, $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $all, $size
boolean$eq, $ne, $in, $nin, $exists, $all, $size
date$eq, $ne, $in, $nin, $exists, $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $all, $size
id$eq, $ne, $in, $nin, $exists, $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $all, $size
stringset$eq, $ne, $in, $nin, $exists, $startsWith, $endsWith, $containsText, $contains, $all, $size
vector$eq, $ne, $in, $nin, $exists, $all, $size

Values follow the kind: a string for string and id (an enum field takes any string), a number, a boolean, a Date or a date string for date, and any string, number, boolean or Date for stringset and vector; null for every kind. A field takes at most one of $startsWith, $endsWith and $containsText. $and and $or nest at any depth, and $search and $near apply to the whole filter. What null and unset fields match is under Querying. A sort takes 1 or -1 on any field.

Gotchas

  • Undeclared fields are open. A field the model doesn't declare takes any operator and value, so a misspelled field name isn't refused. Check names against the model's interface, Db3.<Model>.
  • A filter typed Record<string, unknown> isn't checked. A filter you build in a variable of that type passes any operator. Type the variable Db3.<Model>Filter to have it checked.
  • Start the opt-in file with export {};. Without that line the declaration replaces the primitive-functions module, and every function that imports from it fails to push.
  • Models shared across types. When two db3 types declare a model with the same fields and TypeScript types, but one field has a different kind (date in one type, string in the other), they share one Db3.<Model> and one filter. That field is open in the filter.

Calling an outside service ​

A function cannot fetch the internet; it calls an integration it declares with an integration:<key> capability, through ctx.integrations.call, and the platform adds the integration's credentials so the function never reads them. Each call is recorded in primitive integrations logs with the run and, inside step.do, the step that made it. See Calling It From a Function.

Running a prompt ​

ctx.prompts.run runs one of the app's saved prompts by key, with no capability to declare. See Running a Prompt From a Function.

Typed, parsed output ​

When the prompt declares [prompt.outputSchema], a successful result also carries parsed, validated against that schema and typed from it. See Typed, Structured Output and, for prompts that answer questions about a state, Decisions models.

Reading secrets and config vars ​

A secret:<NAME> capability lets a function read one app secret by name; config vars need no declaration:

ts
import { defineFunction, requireSignedIn } from "primitive-functions";

export default defineFunction({
  input: [],
  authorize: requireSignedIn(),
  handler: async (_input, ctx) => {
    const region = await ctx.configVar("REGION");
    const token = await ctx.secret("PARTNER_TOKEN");
    return { region, tokenLength: token.length };
  },
});
toml
capabilities = ["secret:PARTNER_TOKEN"]

Two things worth knowing before you reach for ctx.secret:

  • Prefer an integration when the secret is a credential for one. An integration's {{secrets.*}} templates are resolved by the platform into the outbound request, so the value never enters your sandbox at all. ctx.secret is for the cases an integration cannot express.
  • Secrets and config vars are provisioned per environment, out of band from your push. So a secret: capability is checked for spelling at push and for existence at call time: a declared name with no value in this environment answers FUNCTION_SECRET_NOT_FOUND (or FUNCTION_VAR_NOT_FOUND for a var), naming the key so you can set it.

The two namespaces are separate. ctx.secret("X") never reads a config var named X, and ctx.configVar("X") never reads a secret.

Secret values are read through a short stale-while-revalidate cache, so a secret you have just rotated may serve its previous value for up to about a minute. That is the platform's read cache, not a property of your function — a retry a minute later sees the new value.

A function's running instance caches each config var the first time it reads it, with no fixed expiry — it keeps serving that value until a new version is pushed (any change to its code or TOML) or the instance restarts on its own. Because that restart is outside your control, one test call after changing a var does not prove every invocation sees the change; push a new version when you need that guarantee. Missing values are not cached. Secret rotation does not require a push; the new value becomes available after the short secret cache refreshes.

Sending to a connected client ​

ctx.users.send and ctx.connections.send push a message to a client that is connected right now, with nothing to declare:

ts
import { defineFunction, requireSignedIn } from "primitive-functions";

export default defineFunction({
  input: ["userId"],
  authorize: requireSignedIn(),
  handler: async (input: { userId: string }, ctx) => {
    const result = await ctx.users.send(input.userId, {
      kind: "order-ready",
      orderId: "o-1",
    });
    return { delivered: result.connections };
  },
});

The client receives your payload and the sending function’s key:

ts
client.on("directMessage", (event) => {
  // event.payload is what the function passed; event.functionKey is who sent it
  console.log(event.functionKey, event.payload, event.sentAt);
});
swift
for await event in client.stream(for: DirectMessageEvent.self) {
  // event.payload (JSONValue?) is what the function passed;
  // event.functionKey is who sent it; event.sentAt is when.
  print(event.functionKey, event.sentAt)
  if let message = event.payload?["message"]?.stringValue {
    print(message)
  }
}

What the API promises, and what it deliberately does not:

  • Presence is not guaranteed. A user with no connected client answers { connections: 0, truncated: false } — a success, not an error. There is no durable record behind the frame: a client that was offline does not receive it later. Write a record the client reads if the message has to survive being missed.
  • One socket, one frame. A client with several databases open is one connection, counted once and delivered once.
  • The fanout is bounded at 64 unique connections per user, and the lookup behind it is bounded too. Past either bound the send delivers what it found and answers truncated: true — treat that flag as "there may be more", not as an error.
  • Payloads are capped at 64 KiB serialized. Over it, the call answers 413 naming the bound and nothing is delivered.
  • ctx.connections.send(connectionId, payload) addresses one connection. An id belonging to another app answers exactly as an id that never existed — connection ids are not a way to reach another tenant. A browser tab keeps its connection id across reloads, and each tab has its own, so an id your app stored still reaches the same tab after it reloads.

Channels ​

A direct send addresses a user or a connection you already know. A channel addresses whoever is listening to a named topic — an order's status, a game table, a shared board's presence lane — without your function knowing who that is.

Two calls make one, and neither needs a declaration:

toml
# primitive/dev/functions/order-room.toml
[function]
key = "order-room"
entry = "functions/order-room.ts"

[function.inputSchema]
type = "object"

[function.inputSchema.properties.orderId]
type = "string"
maxLength = 64
ts
import { defineFunction, requireSignedIn } from "primitive-functions";

export default defineFunction({
  input: ["orderId"],
  authorize: requireSignedIn(),
  handler: async (input: { orderId: string }, ctx) => {
    // 1. Authorize the caller for one channel. The grant names the CALLER, so it
    //    is not a credential anybody else can use.
    const { grant, expiresAt } = await ctx.channels.authorize(
      `orders:${input.orderId}`
    );
    return { grant, expiresAt };
  },
});

The client subscribes with the grant, then receives messages published to the channel:

ts
// 1. Ask the authorizing function for a grant; it names this caller and one channel.
const result = await client.functions.invoke<{ grant: string; expiresAt: number }>(
  "order-room",
  { input: { orderId } }
);
if (result.status !== "completed" || !result.output) return;

// 2. Present the grant on the socket the client already has.
const subscription = await client.subscribeToChannel(
  `orders:${orderId}`,
  result.output.grant
);

client.on("channelMessage", (event) => {
  // event.channel, event.payload, event.functionKey, event.sentAt
  console.log(event.channel, event.payload);
});

// A grant that expired while the socket was down is refused on reconnect with
// nothing waiting on it — invoke the function again and re-subscribe.
client.on("channelSubscribeFailed", (event) => {
  console.warn("renew", event.channel, event.message);
});

// Later: leave. Idempotent — the same as client.unsubscribeFromChannel(channel).
subscription.unsubscribe();
swift
struct Grant: Decodable, Sendable { let grant: String; let expiresAt: Int }

// 1. Ask the authorizing function for a grant; it names this caller and one channel.
let result: FunctionResult<Grant> = try await client.functions.invoke(
  "order-room",
  input: ["orderId": orderId]
)
guard result.status == "completed", let output = result.output else { return }

// 2. Present the grant on the socket the client already has.
let subscription = try await client.subscribeToChannel(
  "orders:\(orderId)",
  grant: output.grant
)

// Later: leave. Idempotent — the same as client.unsubscribeFromChannel(channel).
subscription.unsubscribe()

Publish from a function when an event occurs, for example after saving an order:

ts
await ctx.channels.publish(`orders:${orderId}`, { status: "shipped" });

publish answers { connections, truncated }: how many connections received the frame, and whether the fanout stopped at its ceiling of 500 connections per channel. Zero connections is a success, not an error — nobody was listening.

Channel names ​

A channel name is one or more segments of [A-Za-z0-9_-] joined by :, at most 200 characters — orders, orders:42, orders:42:chat. A name outside the grammar is a 400 about the name (FUNCTION_CHANNEL_NAME_INVALID), decided before anything else.

Expiry is the revocation ​

A grant is a short-lived signed token, not a row, so there is nothing to delete: expiry is the only revocation, and it ends MEMBERSHIP, not just the join.

  • The default TTL is 300 seconds and the ceiling is 900. Ask for more with ctx.channels.authorize(channel, { ttlSeconds }) and you get the ceiling, not an error.
  • expiresAt comes back with the grant so a client can renew ahead of time. Renewing is re-subscribing with a fresh grant: same channel, same socket, new expiry.
  • Past expiresAt the server stops delivering even though the socket is still open. A client that keeps its connection but lets its grant lapse simply stops hearing the channel until it re-subscribes.

Renew by invoking the authorizing function again and re-subscribing with the fresh grant — the same two calls as the first join, timed a minute ahead of expiresAt:

ts
setTimeout(async () => {
  const result = await client.functions.invoke<{ grant: string; expiresAt: number }>(
    "order-room",
    { input: { orderId } }
  );
  if (result.status !== "completed" || !result.output) return;

  await client.subscribeToChannel(`orders:${orderId}`, result.output.grant);
}, expiresAt - Date.now() - 60_000);
swift
struct Grant: Decodable, Sendable { let grant: String; let expiresAt: Int }

let delayMillis = max(0, expiresAt - nowMillis - 60_000)
// Spelled `_Concurrency.Task` because a generated model named `Task` would
// otherwise shadow it — which is easy to hit, since `tasks` is a common
// model name.
try await _Concurrency.Task.sleep(nanoseconds: UInt64(delayMillis) * 1_000_000)

let result: FunctionResult<Grant> = try await client.functions.invoke(
  "order-room",
  input: ["orderId": orderId]
)
guard result.status == "completed", let output = result.output else { return }

_ = try await client.subscribeToChannel("orders:\(orderId)", grant: output.grant)

Invalid grants return the same error, without revealing which validation failed. The error names the requested channel so the client can identify the failed subscription.

On reconnect the client re-issues every subscribe it is holding with its stored grant. A grant that has expired in the meantime is refused, and only that channel's registration is dropped — the client reports it on the channelSubscribeFailed event ({ channel, message }), which is your cue to invoke the authorizing function again and re-subscribe.

A grant is a bearer token for one user

ctx.channels.authorize always names a grantee. An HTTP invocation defaults to its caller; a trigger fire has no caller and must pass { userId } explicitly (FUNCTION_CHANNEL_GRANTEE_REQUIRED otherwise), and a grant is refused at subscribe time if the socket's user is not the one it names. There is no app-wide channel grant.

Inviting people who have no account ​

Use ctx.api.invitations.create to invite an email into the app with nothing else attached. The invitation admits the person to an invite-only app, and they become a member when they sign up. Check first with ctx.api.users.lookup, which answers whether the email already belongs to a member of this app, then send your own email with the returned inviteToken:

ts
const found = await ctx.api.users.lookup({ email: input.email });
if (found.exists) return { userId: found.user?.userId };

const invitation = await ctx.api.invitations.create({ body: { email: input.email } });
const acceptUrl = `https://myapp.example/invite/accept?inviteToken=${invitation.inviteToken}`;
await ctx.api.email.send({
  body: {
    to: input.email,
    subject: "You're invited",
    htmlBody: `<a href="${acceptUrl}">Join the class</a>`,
    textBody: `Join the class: ${acceptUrl}`,
  },
});
return { invitationId: invitation.invitationId };

Keep the invitationId: ctx.api.invitations.get({ invitationId }) returns the invitation with its inviteToken and status, and ctx.api.invitations.delete({ invitationId }) cancels it. ctx.api.invitations.list pages through every invitation in the app. These calls run with the app's authority, so member invitation settings and quotas do not apply.

The person accepts in your app: signing up with the invited email accepts the invitation, and a user signed in under another email accepts the token with client.invitations.accept(inviteToken). Function code cannot accept an invitation.

Gotchas

  • A function invites at role: "member" only; admin or owner answers 403 with errorCode: "FUNCTION_INVITE_MEMBER_ONLY". Promote the person after they sign up with ctx.api.users.setRole, which needs the users:setRolecapability.
  • An email that is already a member answers 400 with errorCode: "USER_ALREADY_MEMBER", and one with a pending invitation INVITATION_PENDING. Emails are stored lowercased, so Ana@Example.com and ana@example.com are the same invitation.
  • sendEmail: true sends the platform's invitation email from the caller. A run with no caller sends nothing and records sys:<appId> as invitedBy, so send your own email.

Sending email ​

Use ctx.api.email.send to send app email. Choose template or inline content, and choose either to or toUserId. A toUserId must belong to this app.

ts
await ctx.api.email.send({
  body: {
    toUserId: input.userId,
    subject: "Your receipt",
    htmlBody: `<p>Thanks, ${input.name}.</p>`,
    textBody: `Thanks, ${input.name}.`,
    variables: { appName: "Acme" },
  },
});

variables fills each {{name}} in the subject and bodies: htmlBody HTML-escapes the value and textBody inserts it as written, so a link arrives intact.

Email sending is available from function code. The function’s authorize method controls who may request it.

The app has ONE hourly email budget; passing it answers 429 with errorCode: "EMAIL_RATE_LIMITED".

Writing analytics for a user ​

Use ctx.api.analytics.writeForUser to attribute an event to a specified user. See Writing events from a server function.

Reading a member's usage ​

ctx.usage.forUser(userId, { since, until }) answers what one member drove in this app over a window, as a quantity per meter, and the bytes they own now. It carries no cost. Naming a member other than the caller follows Naming other members.

ts
const usage = await ctx.usage.forUser(member.userId, { since: new Date(Date.now() - 86_400_000) });
const tokens = usage.meters.find((line) => line.meter === "llm.tokens.in")?.quantity ?? 0;

See Usage for the answer and the window.

Bounded fan-out, ids, and step policies ​

Three helpers ship in primitive-functions:

ts
import { pMap, ulid, stepPolicy } from "primitive-functions";

// Bounded concurrency — an unbounded Promise.all over a page of rows spends
// the sandbox's whole subrequest budget in one line.
const results = await pMap(rows, (row) => handle(row), { concurrency: 4 });

// Generate ids INSIDE step.do. A task run re-executes its handler on every
// resume and memoizes only what a step returned, so an id minted at the top of
// a handler is a different id after a sleep.
const id = await step.do("mint-id", async () => ulid());

// The platform's timeout and retry policy for non-idempotent calls.
// `retries: 0` on email and the AI families is deliberate: a retried timeout
// would send the same email twice or bill the same generation twice.
await step.do("send-receipt", stepPolicy.email, () =>
  ctx.api.email.send({ body: { to, subject, htmlBody } })
);

stepPolicy carries email, llm, gemini and database. It is a default you apply, not a policy the engine forces on your own step.do calls.

step.do accepts a StepConfig: { retries?: { limit, delay, backoff? }, timeout? }. The generated types reject unrecognized options, such as retry instead of retries.

Following up on a write ​

Perform follow-up work in the function that writes the record: save, then publish a message or start another task.

ts
// primitive/dev/functions/place-order/index.ts
import { defineFunction, requireSignedIn } from "primitive-functions";

export default defineFunction("place-order", {
  input: ["db3Id", "orderId", "label"],
  authorize: requireSignedIn(),
  handler: async (input: { db3Id: string; orderId: string; label: string }, ctx) => {
    const { record } = await ctx.db3(input.db3Id, "orders").model("orders").save({
      id: input.orderId,
      data: { label: input.label },
    });

    // …then publish, in the same handler, with the saved record in hand.
    await ctx.channels.publish(`orders:${record.id}`, { op: "save", label: record.label });

    // …or write another database, notify, call an integration — whatever the
    // write was FOR.
    await ctx.db3(input.db3Id, "orders").model("shipments").save({ data: { orderId: record.id } });

    return { placed: record.id };
  },
});

If the follow-up is slow — a long fan-out, a call that may take minutes — hand it to a task rather than making the caller wait:

ts
await ctx.functions.start(
  "reconcile-order",
  { orderId: input.orderId },
  { runKey: `reconcile-${input.orderId}` }
);

Await follow-up calls so their failures are visible to the caller.

Capabilities ​

Capabilities opt a function into integrations, secret values, and selected operations such as creating or deleting resources:

KindWhat it configures
integration:<key>The egress allowlist — which integrations ctx.integrations.call may reach.
secret:<NAME>Which secret values may enter the sandbox through ctx.secret.
Resource and permission changesOperations that destroy something, hand out persistent authority, or provision a resource.
users:readAny, users:actAsAnyNaming another member on a call about one user, in a run a plain member invoked.
tokens:signSigning action links with ctx.actionTokens.sign.

Declare these capabilities when using the corresponding operations:

OperationCapability
users.setRoleusers:setRole
blobBuckets.createBucket / blobBuckets.deleteBucketblobBuckets:createBucket / blobBuckets:deleteBucket
db3.setSync (turn a database's sync on or off)db3:setSync
db3.transfer (move a database to another member or to the app)db3:transfer
db3.setOwnerRow (remove or restore a database holder's owner row)db3:setOwnerRow
db3.setAppAccess (grant a database to every user of the app)db3:setAppAccess
db3.setPublicAccess (mark a database public, or clear it)db3:setPublicAccess
toml
# primitive/dev/functions/provision.toml
[function]
key = "provision"
entry = "functions/provision/index.ts"
capabilities = ["db3:setAppAccess", "integration:stripe", "secret:PARTNER_TOKEN"]
ts
// functions/provision/index.ts
import { defineFunction, requireRole } from "primitive-functions";

export default defineFunction({
  input: [],
  authorize: requireRole("admin"),
  handler: async (input, ctx) => {
    /* ... */
  },
});

A call without its required capability fails and names the missing value. Capabilities belong to the running function version. Operation-specific rules still apply; for example, users.setRole cannot change the app owner.

Naming other members ​

A run that an ordinary member invoked may name only its caller on a call that is about one user. A function that needs another member's data, with the member chosen by its own code, declares one or both of:

CapabilityLets a member-invoked run name another member on
users:readAnyReads: groups.listUserMemberships, collections.list and listForUser, a member's db3s, owned and shared, agentSessions.list, resolving or opening a user alias, a member's holdings (listByCustodian with user:<id>), and a member's usage (ctx.usage.forUser).
users:actAsAnyCalls that act as the member: ctx.agents session calls other than listSessions; ctx.db3(id, type, { asUser }); setting or deleting a user alias, and creating a db3 with one.
toml
# primitive/dev/functions/remove-member.toml
[function]
key = "remove-member"
entry = "functions/remove-member/index.ts"
capabilities = ["users:readAny"]
ts
// The student comes from the class's own groups, never from input.
const memberships = await ctx.api.groups.listUserMemberships({ userId: student.userId });

Each capability covers only its own kind of call: users:readAny does not let a run open a member's database as that member. Neither applies to a run an agent drives, which still names only its initiator, or to the app's own holdings (listByCustodian with app). A function started with ctx.functions.start runs on its own capabilities, not its parent's.

Gotchas:

  • Choose the member in code, not from input. Any member who may invoke a function holding one of these capabilities can reach any member it names. Take the user id from your own data, or check it before the call.

Nothing else is declared — a database's records, a prompt, a config var, a channel, a send, an email, an analytics write are all reachable on the app's authority.

Push validates capability names and requires referenced integrations to exist. Secret values are set separately for each environment; reading an unset secret returns FUNCTION_SECRET_NOT_FOUND.

Anything else answers a structured error you can catch:

errorCodeMeaning
FUNCTION_EGRESS_DENIEDfetch to a host other than the platform.
FUNCTION_ROUTE_NOT_ALLOWEDA platform route not published to functions.
FUNCTION_INTEGRATION_GRANT_MISSINGAn integration call the function's capabilities do not cover. The message names the string that would.
FUNCTION_SECRET_GRANT_MISSINGA secret read the function's capabilities do not cover.
FUNCTION_HIGH_BLAST_GRANT_MISSINGA high-blast operation the function's capabilities do not cover. The message names the exact string.
FUNCTION_SECRET_NOT_FOUNDThe capability is declared; this environment has no secret of that name.
FUNCTION_VAR_NOT_FOUNDThis environment has no config var of that name.
FUNCTION_SEND_TARGET_NOT_FOUNDThe user is not a member of this app, or the connection is not one of this app's.
FUNCTION_SEND_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGEA send payload over the 64 KiB ceiling. Nothing was delivered.
FUNCTION_SUBJECT_REQUIREDA call about one user, from a run with no caller, named no userId.
SUBJECT_USER_INVALIDA call about one user passed a userId that is empty, null or not a user id. Omit it to mean the caller.
SUBJECT_USER_FORBIDDENThe run may not name a user other than its caller: a member invoked it and the function does not declare users:readAny (reads) or users:actAsAny (acting as the member), or an agent drives it.
SUBJECT_USER_NOT_FOUNDThe userId an optional-userId call or ctx.usage.forUser names is not a member of this app. Of the other reads that require a userId, groups.listUserMemberships answers an empty list and the rest a plain 404 with no code.
FUNCTION_CHANNEL_GRANTEE_REQUIREDctx.channels.authorize from a trigger fire with no userId — there is no caller to default to.
FUNCTION_CHANNEL_NAME_INVALIDA channel name outside the grammar.
FUNCTION_CHANNEL_GRANTEE_NOT_FOUNDThe userId a grant names is not a member of this app — the same answer as a user that never existed.
QUERY_IN_LIST_TOO_LARGEA single $in or $nin list over 1 000 values. The message names the field, the count and the cap. See Limits.
QUERY_FILTER_TOO_MANY_BINDSA query whose statement would bind more than 100 parameters. The message names the bound and the count. An $or of equality branches on the same fields costs one parameter between them, as an $in list does; anything else has to be narrowed or split.
